title: Explain the SOLID principles
prompt: Explain the five SOLID principles of object-oriented design. For each principle, give a one-line description and a short concrete example of the problem it prevents.
hints: Single Responsibility and Interface Segregation both deal with keeping units focused.
Open/Closed is about adding new behavior without editing existing code.
Liskov Substitution is about not breaking the contracts promised by the base class.
idealAnswer: SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles. Single Responsibility: a class should have only one reason to change. Open/Closed: a class should be open for extension but closed for modification. Liskov Substitution: a subclass must be substitutable for its base class without breaking behavior. Interface Segregation: prefer many small, focused interfaces over one large interface. Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions rather than concrete implementations. Following these principles yields code that is easier to test, extend, and maintain.
keyPoints: Single Responsibility: one reason to change
Open/Closed: extend without modifying
Liskov Substitution: substitutable subclasses
Interface Segregation: small focused interfaces
Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions

title: Describe common design patterns and when to use them
prompt: Explain the Strategy, Observer, and Factory design patterns. For each pattern, describe the problem it solves and a real-world situation where you would use it.
hints: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface.
Observer decouples a subject from its dependents, like event listeners.
Factory centralizes object creation when construction is complex or varies.
idealAnswer: Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, each in its own class behind a common interface, so the calling code can swap behavior at runtime; use it for payment methods, sorting strategies, or validation rules. Observer lets one subject notify many dependents of state changes without coupling them; use it for event systems, UI updates, or pub/sub. Factory (factory method or abstract factory) centralizes object creation, hiding construction details and conditional logic; use it when creating objects is complex, varies, or depends on configuration. Patterns give us proven vocabulary and structure, but they should be applied only where they actually reduce complexity.
keyPoints: Strategy: interchangeable algorithms swapped at runtime
Observer: one-to-many notifications with loose coupling
Factory: centralized object creation for complex or varying construction
Patterns are tools, not goals: apply only where they reduce complexity

title: Time vs. space complexity tradeoffs
prompt: Explain the tradeoff between time complexity and space complexity. Give one example where using more memory reduces time, and one where using less memory costs more time.
hints: Memoization and caching are classic time-for-space trades.
In-place, iterative solutions often trade time for less memory.
idealAnswer: Time complexity describes how runtime grows with input size; space complexity describes how memory grows. Many problems allow a tradeoff: using extra memory such as caches, hash maps, or precomputed tables can reduce time, while space-constrained solutions often recompute work. Example: finding a duplicate in an array is O(n^2) with brute force but O(n) time and O(n) space with a hash set. Conversely, computing Fibonacci with memoization uses O(n) space for O(n) time, while a plain recursive version is exponential in time with O(n) stack space. The right balance depends on the constraints, data size, and hardware.
keyPoints: Time complexity measures growth of runtime; space measures memory growth
Hash maps and caches trade memory for faster lookups
In-place and iterative solutions trade time for less memory
Choose the balance based on constraints and expected input size

title: The testing pyramid
prompt: Explain the testing pyramid and why the distribution of tests matters. Where do unit, integration, and end-to-end tests belong, and why?
hints: The base is many fast, isolated unit tests.
The top is a few slow, end-to-end tests.
The middle layer holds a moderate number of integration tests.
idealAnswer: The testing pyramid is a model for distributing tests: a wide base of many fast unit tests, a smaller middle layer of integration tests, and a tiny top of end-to-end tests. Unit tests are fast, isolated, and pinpoint failures precisely, so we want many of them. Integration tests verify that components work together with databases, APIs, or external services and are slower. End-to-end tests validate complete user flows through the real system but are slow and brittle, so they should be few and reserved for the most critical journeys. Following the pyramid keeps the suite fast, stable, and maintainable while maximizing coverage per unit of test cost.
keyPoints: Unit tests: many, fast, isolated; the base of the pyramid
Integration tests: moderate number, verify components together
End-to-end tests: few, slow, reserved for critical flows
A correct distribution keeps suites fast and reliable

title: Refactoring and code smells
prompt: What is refactoring? Name at least three common code smells and explain how you would fix each one.
hints: Duplicated code and long methods are usually resolved by extraction.
Refactoring changes structure without changing observable behavior.
Run the test suite before and after each small refactoring step.
idealAnswer: Refactoring is restructuring existing code to improve readability, maintainability, and design without changing its observable behavior, ideally with a passing test suite before and after. Common smells include duplicate code, fixed by extracting a shared method or function; long methods or classes, split by responsibility; large parameter lists, replaced with a parameter object or builder; and feature envy or god classes, fixed by moving responsibilities to the correct owner. Refactoring should be done in small, behavior-preserving steps with tests guarding every step so regressions are caught immediately.
keyPoints: Refactoring preserves behavior while improving structure
Duplicate code: extract shared logic
Long methods and classes: split by responsibility
Large parameter lists: introduce a parameter object
Run tests before and after each refactoring step

title: Agile practices and estimation
prompt: Describe key Agile practices, such as Scrum ceremonies or XP habits, and explain how you would estimate work using story points and planning poker.
hints: Estimation is about relative size and uncertainty, not exact hours.
Velocity, measured over sprints, converts points into delivery forecasts.
idealAnswer: Agile emphasizes iterative delivery, continuous feedback, and adaptability. Common practices include short sprints, daily stand-ups, sprint planning, sprint reviews, and retrospectives, plus engineering habits such as test-driven development and continuous integration. Estimation usually uses story points with planning poker: the team compares stories relatively and reaches consensus on size. Points measure relative size and uncertainty rather than time, and velocity lets the team predict how much it can deliver per iteration. Estimation should be done by the people doing the work and refined as the team learns.
keyPoints: Practices: sprints, stand-ups, planning, reviews, retrospectives
Story points measure relative size and uncertainty
Planning poker drives consensus among the team
Velocity turns estimates into delivery forecasts
The team that does the work does the estimating

The first value you see twice is the answer.

hints: Compare characters position by position across all strings.
Stop at the shortest string or at the first mismatch.

hints: The sum 0 + 1 + ... + n minus the sum of the array gives the missing number.
